original_value: This study presents a straightforward method to teach robots to use tools. Teaching robots is crucial in quickly deploying and reconfiguring robots in next‐generation factories. Conventional methods require third‐party systems like wearable devices or complicated vision system to capture, analyse, and map human grasps, motion, and tool poses to robots. These systems assume lots of experience from their users. Unlike the conventional methods, this study does not involve learning human motion and skills. Instead, it only learns the object goal poses from the human user whilst employs regrasp planning to generate robot motion. The method is most suitable for a robot to learn the usage of electric tools that can be operated by simply switching on and off. The proposed method is validated using a dual‐arm robot with hand‐mounted cameras and several tools. Experimental results show that the proposed method is robust, feasible, and simple to teach robots. It can find a collision‐free and kino‐dynamic feasible grasp sequences and motion trajectories when the goal pose is reachable. The method allows the robot to automatically choose placements or handover considering the surrounding environment as intermediate states to change the pose of the tool and use tools following human demonstrations.

result.paraphrase: This study introduces a simple approach for teaching robots to use tools. Robot teaching is important for rapidly deploying and reconfiguring robots in next-generation factories. Conventional methods rely on third-party systems such as wearable devices or complex vision systems to capture, analyze, and map human grasps, motions, and tool poses to robots, and these systems require substantial user expertise. In contrast, this study does not learn human motion or skills. It learns only the object goal poses from the human user and uses regrasp planning to generate robot motion. The method is best suited to robots learning how to use electric tools that can be operated by simply switching them on and off. The proposed method is evaluated with a dual-arm robot equipped with hand-mounted cameras and several tools. Experimental results indicate that the method is robust, feasible, and easy to teach to robots. When the goal pose is reachable, it can find collision-free, kino-dynamically feasible grasp sequences and motion trajectories. It also enables the robot to automatically choose placements or handovers based on the surrounding environment as intermediate states to change the tool pose and use tools according to human demonstrations.
